8.8 Skin Impairment Evaluation Summary

Introduction

This chapter provides criteria for evaluating perma-nent impairment of the skin and its appendages and estimating the extent to which skin impairments affect the ability to perform Activities of Daily Living, or ADLs (see Table 1-2). Permanent impairment of the skin is any dermatologic abnormality or loss that persists after medical treatment and rehabilitation, is unlikely to change significantly in the next year with or without medical treatment, and affects ADLs.

Table 8-1 summarizes skin components, functions, and disorders. Skin functions include: (1) providing a protective covering; (2) participating in sensory perception, temperature regulation, fluid regulation, electrolyte balance, immunobiologic defenses, and trauma resistance; and (3) regenerating the epidermis and its appendages.1

Protective skin functions include barrier defenses against chemical irritants and allergic sensitizer damage, microorganism invasion, and ultraviolet light injuries. Temperature regulation involves proper functioning of sweat glands and small blood vessels. The barrier defense against fluid loss is related to the intactness of the stratum corneum.

8.1 Principles of Assessment

Before using the information in this chapter, the Guides user should become familiar with Chapters 1 and 2 and the Glossary. Chapters 1 and 2 discuss the Guides’ purpose, applications, and methods for per-forming and reporting impairment evaluations. The Glossary provides definitions of common terms used by many specialties in impairment evaluation.

Skin disorders may develop from exposure to physi-cal, mechanical, biological, and chemical agents. Identification and avoidance of these agents may pre-vent ongoing skin disorder aggravation. Physicians need to determine the clinical course and perma-nence of skin disorders associated with possible intermittent exposures.

Clinical evaluation requires sound clinical judg-ment based on a detailed medical history, thorough

physical examination, and judicious use of diagnostic procedures. Ancillary diagnostic and laboratory pro-cedures include patch, open, prick, intracutaneous, and serologic allergy tests; Wood’s light examinations; cultures and scrapings for bacteria, fungi, and viruses; and biopsies.1

To determine the appropriate impairment class (Table 8-2) for an affected individual, first evalu-ate the severity of the skin condition; the frequency, intensity, and complexity of the medical condition and treatment regimen; and the impact of the skin condition on the ability to perform ADLs. Burden of Treatment Compliance (BOTC) can be significant in dermatologic disorders, with patients being required to soak affected skin daily, apply topical medications to large areas of the body on a regular basis, avoid sun exposure, or present to the dermatology office several times weekly for phototherapy. This BOTC can affect the ability of patients to complete ADLs and should be considered in the history when ini-tially determining the appropriate impairment class.

After defining the class of impairment using these fac-tors, consider the physical exam and diagnostic testing to determine the exact number in the class that best represents the individual. The skin impairment

ratings are all provided in terms of whole person impairment. All patients must be accurately diagnosed using the evaluation summary found in Table 8-3 before an impairment rating is provided.

The maximum impairment rating for skin disease in this edition of the Guides is 58%. Patients with severe skin disease are likely to experience higher levels of impairment than this rating, but in these situations, it would be expected that other body systems are impaired as a result of the skin disease. Examples would include musculoskeletal impair-ment due to loss of joint mobility in scleroderma or epidermolysis bullosa, arthritis associated with severe psoriasis, and difficulty eating due to oral or esophageal involvement of pemphigus vulgaris.

When a patient experiences a permanent impairment of other body systems, such as restriction of motion or ankylosis of joints, respiratory, cardiovascular, endocrine, or gastrointestinal tract disorders, then the rater should evaluate the extent of whole person impairment related to each system. The rater should then combine the estimated impairment percentages (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix) to determine total impairment.

8.1a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

In some cases, limitations in the ability to perform daily activities are based on symptoms. This infor-mation may be subjective and possibly misinter-preted, and it should not serve as the sole criterion for impairment rating decisions. Rather, obtain objective data about the extent of the limitation and integrate findings with subjective data to estimate the permanent impairment rating.

Objective Testing

A number of dermatology-specific quality-of-life indexes exist, such as the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI),2 the Skindex-16, and the Skindex-29.3 In addition, there are a number of disease-specific severity and quality-of-life indexes, such as the SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) scale and the Psoriasis Disability Index (PDI).4,5 All have been successfully used and validated in the research set-ting, but none have been widely accepted for use in clinical practice, and therefore these scales have not been incorporated into Table 8-2.

Pruritus

Pruritus is a common symptom of dermatologic conditions. Pruritus is a subjective, unpleasant sensation and symptom that provokes the desire to scratch and rub the skin. The itching sensation may

be intolerable. Like pain, pruritus may be defined as a unique complex of afferent stimuli that interacts with the individual’s emotional or affective state of mind.1 Peripheral neural stimulation varies from absence of sensation to awareness that stimuli are producing a usual or unusual sensation. Central nervous system reaction is modified by the state of attentiveness, experience, motivation at the moment, and stimuli such as exercise, sweat, and temperature change.

When evaluating pruritus associated with skin dis-orders, consider (1) how the pruritus interferes with performance of the ADLs and (2) to what extent the pruritus description is supported by such objective skin signs as lichenification, excoriation, or hyper-pigmentation. Subjective itching complaints that can-not be substantiated objectively may require referral or consultation.

8.1b Description of Procedures

Common clinical investigations for dermatologic conditions include skin testing, biopsy, and relevant laboratory studies.

Patch Testing: Performance, Interpretation, and Relevance6

The sine qua non for the diagnosis of allergic contact dermatitis is a properly performed and interpreted patch test. The information from patch testing com-plements an appropriate, detailed history. Patch test-ing may significantly contribute to the diagnosis and management of contact dermatitis.

Be aware that patch testing may yield false-posi-tive and false-negative results. Selecting the proper concentration of the suspected allergen, vehicle, site of application, and type of patch test is critical for procedure validity. Making such selections and determining the relevance of test results require con-siderable skill and experience.

Interpret a positive or negative patch test result in conjunction with the clinical history and a detailed knowledge of testing procedures. Although appropri-ate test concentrations and vehicles have been estab-lished for many sensitizers, there are no established vehicle and concentration standards for many of the chemicals in use.

Patch test results require careful interpretation to discern allergic from irritant responses, as well as to appropriately interpret whether the result is relevant to the individual’s dermatitis and expo-sures. When a positive patch test occurs, the physi-cian must determine if the allergen has definite, probable, possible, past, or unknown relevance to

the patient’s dermatitis. Allergens to which the patient is definitely exposed and for which the areas of exposure correlate with the areas affected with dermatitis are graded as definitely relevant. If, based on known exposures, it is highly likely that the patient is exposed to the allergen in areas affected by dermatitis, then the relevance is graded as probable. If there are possible exposures to the allergen, but exposure cannot be confirmed, then relevance is graded as possible. If no exposures to the allergen can be identified, then relevance is graded as unknown, as it is impossible to rule out the possibility of exposure.

For example, a patient with hand dermatitis is patch tested and found to be allergic to a rubber accelerator.

1. If the manufacturer confirms that the gloves the patient wears contain the accelerator and the patient reacts positively to a patch test with a sample of the glove, then the relevance would be graded as definite.

2. If the manufacturer confirms that the gloves the patient wears contain the accelerator but a glove sample is not available for patch testing, then the relevance would be graded as probable.

3. If it cannot be determined if the gloves contain the accelerator, then the relevance would be graded as possible.

4. If the manufacturer states that the gloves do not contain the accelerator, then the relevance would be graded as unknown, as it is possible that there is a different exposure to the accelerator of which neither the patient nor the physician is aware, or it is possible that the manufacturer is providing incorrect information.

In general, an allergen that is graded as definite, probable, possible, or past relevance is considered to be a relevant positive patch test.

Patch tests are used only to detect contact allergy and are only one component in a complete evalua-tion. Further details about patch testing, its values, and its limitations are discussed in standard texts, some of which are listed in the references at the end of this chapter.

8.2 Disfigurement

Skin disfigurement is an altered or abnormal appear-ance that may be an alteration of color, shape, or structure, or a combination of these. Disfigurement

may be a residual of injury or disease, or it may accompany a recurrent or ongoing disorder. Examples of disfigurement include giant pigmented nevi, nevus flammeus, cavernous hemangioma, and pigmentation alteration. Facial disfigurement is rated in Chapter 11 (Table 11-5). All other disfigurement is rated in this chapter.

Disfigurement usually has no effect on body function and may have little or no effect on the ability to per-form ADLs, except if the disfigurement causes social rejection or an unfavorable self-image with self-imposed isolation, lifestyle alteration, or other behav-ioral changes. If impairment in the ability to perform ADLs due to disfigurement does exist, it may be manifested by a behavior change, such as withdrawal from social contacts. This may be taken into account under Table 8-2 when the examiner believes the behavior is clearly related to severe disfigurement.

Evaluate impairments related to disfigurement or altered pigmentation in accordance with the criteria given in Table 8-2 and described later in this chapter. Describe disfigurement and enhance with good color photographs that show multiple views of the defect. Estimate the probable duration and permanency of the disfigurement. Describe the possibility of improving the condition through medical or surgical therapy and the extent to which it can be concealed cosmetically, as with hairpieces, wigs, or cosmetics. Depict with photographs if possible.

8.3 Scars and Skin Grafts

Scars are cutaneous abnormalities that result from the healing of burned, traumatized, or diseased tissue. They represent a special type of disfigure-ment. Give the scars’ dimensions in centimeters and describe their shape, color, anatomic location, and any evidence of ulceration, depression, or elevation. Indicate whether the scar is atrophic or hypertro-phic; soft and pliable or hard and indurated, thin or thick, and smooth or rough; and whether there is any attachment to underlying bones, joints, muscles, or other tissue. Good color photographs with multiple views of the defect enhance the scars’ description.

Consider the tendency of a scar to disfigure when evaluating whether there is permanent impairment due to scarring. Also consider whether the scar can be changed, made less visible, or concealed. Function may be restored without improving appear-ance, and appearance may be improved without altering function.

Skin grafts may be used to replace skin losses resulting from trauma or disease. Grafts commonly lack hair, lubrication, pliability, and sensation, and they may demonstrate altered pigmentation. These changes affect the function and appearance of the graft site. The altered lubrication, pliability, and sensation may result in diminished protection against microorganisms and diminished resistance to mechanical, chemical, and thermal trauma. The altered appearance may be significant if the area involves exposed parts, such as the dorsum of the hand, the face, or the neck.

If a scar involves the loss of sweat gland function, hair growth, nail growth, or pigment formation, evaluate the effect or effects on the performance of the ADLs. Evaluate burns and scars according to the criteria in this chapter; give special consideration to the injury’s impact on the individual’s ability to perform ADLs. When impairment resulting from a burn or scar is based on peripheral nerve dysfunction or loss of range of motion, evaluate the skin impairment separately and combine the impairment rating with that from Chapter 15, The Upper Extremities; or Chapter 16, The Lower Extremities. If chest wall excursion is limited, consult Chapter 5, The Pulmonary System.

8.4 Contact Dermatitis6–18

Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory skin reaction induced by exposure to an external agent and is the most frequent cause of occupational skin disease. Contact dermatitis most often involves the hands, wrists, and forearms, although any area may be affected. Two types of contact dermatitis are gener-ally recognized: irritant, which results from direct tissue damage, and allergic, in which tissue damage is mediated through type IV delayed cellular hyper-sensitivity. Irritant and allergic contact dermatitis may coexist in the same person and are often dif-ficult to differentiate on physical examination and on histopathology.

Irritants may be strong (absolute) or weak (marginal). Cumulative exposure to marginal irritants causes most cases of irritant contact dermatitis and may impair the barrier function of the skin, allowing the penetration of potential allergens. Many cutaneous allergens, such as chromates, nickel salts, epoxy resins, and preservatives, are also primary irritants. Allergy can be induced or maintained by chemicals in concentrations insufficient to irritate nonallergic skin.

Allergen cross-sensitivity is an important phenom-enon in which an individual who is allergic to one chemical (eg, urushiol in poison ivy or poison oak) also will react to structurally related chemicals (eg, in Japanese lacquer, mango, and cashew nutshell oil).

Accurate diagnosis is the key to proper management of contact dermatitis. If the specific agent or agents can be identified (see Section 8.1b on patch testing) and successfully avoided, full recovery is antici-pated. However, if contact continues, the dermatitis may become chronic and disabling, and it may pre-vent the individual from performing some ADLs. It should be noted that in rare cases, especially those involving occupational allergy to chromates, there can be long-term persistence of dermatitis, despite avoidance of all known sources of the allergen.19

Three special situations should be considered in contact dermatitis. First, patients who have special-ized occupations and who develop severe contact dermatitis may be unable to continue working in their occupation. In this setting, the patient may no longer have any active dermatitis after being removed from the work environment; however, they have clearly experienced a permanent immunologic change that may affect them in the future and that has limited their employment opportunities. For the permanent change in cutaneous immunology and physiology, they should receive 3% impairment if they have not met any other criteria in Table 8-2 for a rating and the chemical is one they may encounter in other settings.

The second special situation is the patient with an occupational contact dermatitis who continues to have dermatitis because that person continues to work but whose disease would be expected to clear completely if he or she stopped working. In this set-ting, once all reasonable workplace accommodations have been made, if the dermatitis continues despite therapy, the patient should be rated in his or her cur-rent condition with the assumption that the patient has reached maximum medical improvement (MMI).

The third special situation is the patient with extreme sensitivity to a relevant allergen or with sensitivity to multiple relevant allergens. In these situations, it is anticipated that the number of allergies or degree of allergy would lead to greater restrictions in the patient’s activities than a patient with a lower sensi-tivity or with allergy to only a single substance, and hence that the allergies would have a greater impact on the patient’s ability to perform ADLs. This is reflected in the “Diagnostic Test Findings” portion of Table 8-2.

8.5 Natural Rubber Latex Allergy20–24

Latex allergy generally refers to an immunoglobu-lin E (IgE)-mediated immediate hypersensitivity reaction to one or more protein allergens present in natural rubber latex (NRL) devices, especially gloves. Individuals with spina bifida and health care workers are at particular risk. Allergy to NRL has become a significant medical and occupational health problem. Clinical manifestations range from contact urticaria and angioedema to allergic rhini-tis and conjunctivitis, asthma, and anaphylaxis. A number of NRL-allergic individuals are atopic, with asthma, other environmental type I allergies, and hand eczema. Symptoms and signs of contact urti-caria to NRL may be masked by preexisting hand eczema. Also evaluate individuals with NRL allergy for manifestations in other organ systems (eg, respi-ratory symptoms and asthma). Contact dermatitis to rubber accelerators and antioxidants added during manufacture has also been associated with NRL exposure.

Allergen avoidance is the current treatment of NRL allergy and contact dermatitis. Glove powder (an NRL-allergen carrier) can produce respiratory symp-toms in susceptible individuals. Affected workers may have to avoid contact with NRL gloves and other NRL-containing products, avoid areas where they might inhale the powder from NRL gloves worn by other workers, and wear a medical alert bracelet. All health care facilities should use nonlatex gloves where possible. When latex gloves must be used, they should be nonpowdered.

8.6 Skin Cancer1

Skin cancer is the most prevalent of all cancers. Three main types exist: basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and malignant melanoma. In the early 21st century, it is estimated that there were 800,000 basal cell carcinomas and 200,000 cutaneous SCCs diagnosed per year. In the year 2004, it is estimated that there were approxi-mately 100,000 melanomas diagnosed, with slightly less than half of these being in situ at diagnosis. Predisposing factors include light skin color, inabil-ity to tan, sun exposure, blond or red hair, freck-ling in childhood, and therapeutic radiation. Each type of skin cancer (BCC, SCC, and melanoma) has several different clinical and histologic types. There is also a much less common, inherited

condition called the basal cell nevus syndrome or Gorlin syndrome in which patients develop hun-dreds or thousands of basal cell carcinomas starting at a relatively young age.

Basal cell carcinoma is usually locally invasive, with a small metastatic potential. The goal of therapy is complete eradication of the tumor, using either surgical techniques, destructive techniques, or topically applied agents, with the least amount of disfigurement.

Squamous cell carcinoma is more common in indi-viduals with light skin coloration. Long-term sun exposure typically leads to precancerous actinic keratoses which may progress to SCC. In addition to sunlight, other environmental risk factors include arsenic, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon, chronic infrared heat, and therapeutic radiation exposure. Additionally, SCC may occur in chronic scars from burns, trauma, and inflammatory processes. Several clinical and histologic types exist, but SCC is more likely to metastasize than is BCC. The risk of SCC metastasis is especially high for neoplasms arising on the lip or ear, as well as in larger, deeper, and more anaplastic lesions. Therapeutic options are the same as for basal cell carcinoma. Sun avoid-ance and close follow-up are essential in patients with SCC.

Cutaneous malignant melanoma is an increasingly common and lethal malignancy of melanocytes and nevus cells. The increasing frequency of melanoma is well documented—rates of incidence are rising more rapidly for this than for any other cancer. The salient challenge for clinicians is to detect and excise melanoma in its earliest stage, as tumor thickness remains the most important prognostic indicator for this malignancy. Early diagnosis and surgical exci-sion of either in situ or early invasive melanomas are curative in most individuals. Despite advances in chemotherapy and immunotherapy, the efficacy of treatment of advanced melanoma remains limited, and the prognosis of metastatic disease remains poor.

8.7 Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Skin Disorders

To use Table 8-2, follow these steps:

1. Establish the diagnosis using the objective physical exam findings and lab tests. If neces-sary, consult a dermatologist. Table 8-3 provides

suggestions for physical exam findings and lab tests that should be noted. Place the individual in the appropriate class based on the history and focusing on impact of the skin disease on ability to perform ADLs. Begin by selecting the middle number in that class. The classes have discrete numbers. They are not a range. You will need to consider the percentage of time that symptoms are present and the amount of treat-ment required. Facial disfigurement is rated in the Ear, Nose, and Throat chapter in Table 11-5. Scars and burns are present permanently; there-fore, time is not a factor considered in the rating. When different elements of the history would lead to placement in different classes (eg, when the impact on ADLs is out of proportion to the frequency of symptoms), the overriding factor should remain objectively established interfer-ence with ADLs. Individuals with mild interfer-ence in ADLs would be unable to engage in or must seriously diminish engagement in nones-sential ADLs, such as previously performed recreational activities. Individuals with moderate interference in daily-living activities would, in addition to the above, have significantly limited ability to perform some essential ADLs, such as bathing or household tasks. Individuals with severe interference with ADLs would be unable to perform many essential ADLs and would be expected to have serious limitations in the abil-ity to maintain employment.

2. Assess the correct class for the physical exam findings. If the class selected is 1 class higher than the class selected from step 1, move up 1 number higher within the class selected using the history. If it is 2 levels higher move up 2 levels within the history-selected class only when 2 numbers are available. Otherwise move only to the top number available in the class selected by the history. If the class from the physical exam is

in a lower class than that selected from the his-tory, move the accordant number of steps lower within the class selected from step 1. For class 4, if the physical exam findings are particularly severe, you may move to the highest number. For classes 2, 3, and 4, most ratings are complete at this step.

3. Assess the class of the patient using the diag-nostic findings. If diagnostic test findings are not necessary or are not expected to be positive for the given diagnosis, ignore this step and use the number obtained after assessing the physical exam findings as the final impairment rating. If positive findings are expected for the given diag-nosis, assess the class based on the comparison between the findings in the individual and those expected. Using the number you have arrived at in step 2, move again up or down depending on if the class is lower than the class originally selected by the history or higher than the class originally selected by the history. You may not move out of the class you have originally selected from your history. For example, if the patient were found to be in class 1 originally by the history, you would begin at 5% as the middle number in class 1. If the physical exam were in class 3, you would move up to 9%, staying within class 1 but moving up 2 numbers. If the diagnostic test were in class 2, it is 1 class higher than the original class, but it would not change your rating since you can-not exceed 9% and remain within class 1. On the other hand, if the diagnostic tests were in a class 0, you would move down 1 step and the final rating would be 7%.

4. Ratings that begin in class 4 are an exception because there are no classes higher than 4; there-fore, the rating increases by 1 category whenever the physical exam or diagnostic findings are also in category 4.

EXAMPLE 8-1: ALLERGIC CONTACT DERMATITIS

Subject: 27-year-old man.

History: Prepared batches of latex paint for small paint manufacturing company. Had related skin dis-ease onset and exacerbation. Despite some accom-modations, individual unable to avoid latex paint completely; dermatitis continued. No dermatitis for 1 year after job change.

Current Symptoms: None.

Physical Exam: Hands and arms: no signs of dermatitis.

Clinical Studies: Patch test: 2+ relevant positive reaction to 0.1% petrolatum mixture of a nonmercurial preservative, 2-n-4-isothiazolin-3-one, used in the company’s latex paints, not allergic to methylisochlorothiazolinone or methylisothiazolinone.

Diagnosis: Resolved allergic contact dermatitis caused by preservative.

Impairment Rating: 0% impairment of the whole person. History places this case in class 0 since skin findings are no longer present.

Comment: While used widely in paint manufac-turing, the preservative is not widely used in other industries, nor is it used in personal care products. While the allergy to the preservative prevents him from performing this particular job, it does not significantly limit his ability to be gain-fully employed, so this ADL is not significantly impaired. There is no limitation in the perfor-mance of other daily activities. Latex paint does not contain NRL allergens and does not cause NRL allergy. No additional rating is provided, as it is unlikely the individual will encounter this chemical in other settings. Patch test is graded as probably relevant, as the preservative is confirmed to be present in the paint to which his hands were exposed. It is not possible to patch test with a sam-ple of the paint the patient used, so the examiner cannot conclude definite relevance, however both probably and definitely relevant patch test reac-tions are considered RPPTRs, so this distinction is not important in determining a rating.

EXAMPLE 8-2: THERMAL BURN SCARRING

Subject: 38-year-old woman.

History: Second-degree flame burn to forearm; spontaneously healed.

Current Symptoms: None. No interference with ADLs.

Physical Exam: 7 × 12-cm depigmented area of the arm. Healed skin: normal pliability, hair, lubrication, and sensation.

Clinical Studies: None.

Diagnosis: Scarring caused by thermal burn.

Impairment Rating: 0% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: No interference with ADLs.

CLASS 1 1% to 9% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 8-3: OCCUPATIONAL LEUKODERMA

Subject: 52-year-old man.

History: Janitor; 13 years’ transient hand dermatitis from wet work with detergents, including germi-cidal disinfectant with para-tert-butyl-phenol (TBP). Developed depigmentation on sides of most fingers, dorsa of the hands, and distal forearms 10 years ago. Recent depigmentation of portions of the upper torso and thighs. Psoralen plus ultraviolet A (PUVA) light therapy with oral methoxsalen 2x per week for over 1 year failed to stimulate repigmentation. Cosmetic covering was unsatisfactory. Required outdoor main-tenance work resulted in frequent sunburn of skin that lacked pigmentation; needs frequent and regular use of protective sunscreen, averaging twice a day during sunny times.

Current Symptoms: None.

Physical Exam: Depigmentation covering less than 10% of the body. Early actinic changes with skin wrinkling, bruising, and scaling.

Clinical Studies: Patch testing showed no positive results.

Diagnosis: Depigmentation, most likely occupa-tional leukoderma.

Impairment Rating: 5% impairment of the whole person due to occupational leukoderma. The rating begins in class 1 at 5%, the middle number, based on the history of the presence of a skin disorder and the need for sunscreen and sun avoidance. The physical exam findings fit a class 1, and thus the rating does not change, staying at 5%. No diagnostic test findings are expected, so this portion of the impairment rating table does not affect the final rating, which remains at 5%.

Comment: Occupational leukoderma is a difficult diagnosis to confirm. Although patch testing with the causative chemical will sometimes lead to depig-mentation, this is not a reliable occurrence and test-ing is not well standardized. Therefore, no positive diagnostic test results are required for the diagnosis of chemical leukoderma, and this element is there-fore not considered in determining a rating.

EXAMPLE 8-4: THERMAL BURN WITH HYPERTROPHIC SCARRING

Subject: 43-year-old man.

History: Healed second-degree burn of anterior part of neck; hypertrophic scar formation involves approximately 1% of body surface area (BSA). Itching and burning temporarily interrupt some ADLs. Treatment with topical steroids is required several times per month.

Current Symptoms: Scar susceptible to ultraviolet light; wears sunscreen when outdoors. Scar easily irritated and lacks durability; patient unable to wear clothes that rub his neck. Intermittent itching and burning episodes confined to scarred areas stops all activities for 5 to 10 minutes.

Physical Exam: Scar raised, red, and hard and con-trasts markedly with adjacent normal skin. Limited neck flexion, extension.

Clinical Studies: None.

Diagnosis: Hypertrophic scar secondary to thermal burn; limitation of neck motion.

Impairment Rating: 7% impairment of the whole person. Daily living activities, such as shaving, bath-ing, and dressing are frequently interrupted due to scar irritation, but only to a minimal degree and area involved is only 1%. Rating begins in class 1 at 5%. The rating is increased by 1 step because the physi-cal exam findings are in class 2 due to involvement of the anterior part of the neck, which is difficult or impossible to conceal. No diagnostic tests are neces-sary, so the final rating is 7%.

EXAMPLE 8-5: CHRONIC HAND DERMATITIS

Subject: 28-year-old woman.

History: Eczematous eruption beneath wedding ring on fourth finger of left hand began shortly after birth of first child 6 years earlier. Gradually spread to areas on several fingers of both hands despite treatment and avoidance of jewelry use. Eruption persisted for several months, then subsided slowly. Severe hand dermatitis flare-up after birth of second child 2 years later, which followed a similar pattern. No eczema, hay fever, or asthma; no family history of atopy.

Current Symptoms: Good general health. Chronic, low-grade dermatitis despite special precautions.

Regular glove use and moisturizer application required to prevent dermatitis flares. Needs to use topical steroids approximately once per month when dermatitis flares. Chronic hand dermatitis causes pain and burning of hands at least several times a week.

Physical Exam: Lichenification on dorsal hands; otherwise normal.

Clinical Studies: Patch test: various food, house-hold, cosmetic, and diagnostic and therapeutic mate-rials nonreactive. A 2+ positive patch test reaction to thimerosal on patch testing.

Diagnosis: Chronic irritant dermatitis of the hands.

Impairment Rating: 7% impairment of the whole person. The combination of minimal interference with ADLs and the need for treatment places the ini-tial rating in class 1 at 5%. The physical exam find-ings are in class 2 due to hand involvement, so the rating is increased to 7%. Because no diagnostic tests are necessary for irritant dermatitis, the category does not affect the rating.

Comment: The patch test reaction to thimerosal is of unknown relevance, as no exposures could be identified. Patch test reactions of unknown relevance are graded as not relevant and are not considered as positive diagnostic test finding.

EXAMPLE 8-6: ALLERGIC CONTACT DERMATITIS

Subject: 32-year old woman.

History: Approximately 5 years earlier the patient began to experience dermatitis after having her hair dyed. She discontinued this practice but began to experience constant itchy eruptions of the eye-lids, face, neck, hands, ears, feet, and upper back. Improved after patch testing and lifestyle modifica-tion to avoid identified allergens. No personal or family history of eczema, hay fever, or asthma.

Current Symptoms: Dermatitis occurs approxi-mately 4 times per year, with each episode being fairly mild and lasting 3 weeks. Main affected areas during flares are eyelids and lateral jaw. During episodes she is quite itchy and requires therapy with prescription topical agents. Between flares, no spe-cific therapy except allergen avoidance is necessary.

Physical Exam: No dermatitis at the time of exam.

Clinical Studies: 1 or 2+ relevant positive patch test reactions (RPPTRs) to cocamidopropyl betaine (CAPB), fragrances, formaldehyde, quaternium-15, DMDM hydantoin, parabens, paraphenylenediamine, carba mix, thiuram mix, lanolin, methylchloroiso-thiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone, para-tert-butyl-phenol formaldehyde resin (PTBFR), and samples of the rubber gloves she wears while washing dishes.

Diagnosis: Allergic contact dermatitis to multiple allergens.

Impairment Rating: Initial rating is in class 1 due to mild severity, need for intermittent topi-cal therapy, and mild interference with ADLs. Physical exam is in class 1 due to transitory nature. Diagnostic test findings are class 3 due to multiple RPPTRs, so rating moves up to 9%.

Comment: This patient has had to significantly curtail performance or have limitations placed on a number of ADLs, such as cleaning the home, groom-ing, clothing selection, shoe selection, glove use, and child care, due to the need to avoid a large number of allergens, as demonstrated by multiple RPPTRs. Major exposures were personal care products such as soap, shampoo, moisturizer, makeup, hair dye, dishwashing liquid, other cleaning products, and personal care products used to care for her children, such as diaper wipes and baby shampoo. She has had to significantly curtail or limit many ADLs that would entail use of these products, including bath-ing her children, a task that her husband now per-forms as a result of her allergies. Reactions to rubber allergens and glues limits her choices of shoes and clothing, which consequently limit the activities in which she can participate. Some of the above reac-tions are considered to be of possible relevance, such as PTBFR, a glue found in shoes. It correlates with the foot dermatitis and is known to be in shoes, but its presence cannot be confirmed in any of her shoes. Other reactions are of possible relevance, such as the quaternium-15, which was confirmed to be present in the baby shampoo she was using to bathe her chil-dren and which therefore correlates with her hand dermatitis. She could not be patch tested to the baby shampoo, so relevance cannot be called definite. The reaction to carba mix and to the kitchen glove is considered definitely relevant, as the manufacturer of the glove confirmed that carba was present in the glove and she reacted directly to a sample of the glove.

EXAMPLE 8-7: ALLERGIC CONTACT DERMATITIS

Subject: 32-year-old man.

History: Construction worker; blistering dermati-tis of hands and feet after work with wet concrete. Severe dermatitis twice treated with oral prednisone. Condition improved away from concrete contact but did not clear completely. Currently, treatment requires administration of a topical agent on most days and 1 to 2 brief courses of prednisone annually.

Current Symptoms: Daily mild, chronic dermatitis of both hands, including palms, with approximately 1 flare a year that necessitates time off from work. Must modify performance of a few specific ADLs, such as dishwashing; has significant limitation of ADLs with flares once per year. Handling dry rock or concrete usually aggravates dermatitis.

Physical Exam: Mild dermatitis of fingers, palms, and feet.

Clinical Studies: Patch test: 2+ to chromate, princi-pal allergen in cement and leather shoes.

Diagnosis: Allergic contact dermatitis to chromate from occupational cement exposure.

Impairment Rating: 9% impairment of the whole person. This rating begins in class 1 at 5% due to the requirement for treatment and minimal interference with ADLs. The physical exam findings are in class 2 due to the involvement of the palmar aspects of the hands. This moves the rating to 7%. The diagnostic test findings are in class 2, so the final rating moves to 9%. If flares causing modifications of ADLs were more frequent, the examiner could consider an ini-tial rating in class 2. Patch test is rated as possibly relevant, because chromate is known to be present in leather and cement, and exposures to these sub-stances correlate with the sites of the rash, but no testing was done to confirm that the actual cement and leather the patient is exposed to contain chro-mate. However, since possibly relevant reactions are graded as RPPTRs, differentiating between possible, probable, or definite relevance does not affect deter-mination of impairment ratings.

EXAMPLE 8-8: LATEX ALLERGY AND ECZEMA

Subject: 38-year-old woman.

History: Dental assistant; 18 years’ progressively worsening chronic hand dermatitis, angioedema of the face, rhinitis, and asthma; flared with powdered NRL gloves. Treatment with topical and systemic corticosteroids. Has history of eczema; jewelry

allergy. Some lotions, creams, and frequent hand washing with antibacterial soap aggravate dermatitis. Nonpowdered NRL gloves cause itching within min-utes, hives on wrists and forearms. Visited urgent care center for disseminated urticaria, angioedema, and wheezing.

Current Symptoms: Temporary improvement with hypoallergenic, powder-free NRL gloves. With no NRL exposure, mild hand dermatitis persists; inter-mittent fingertip fissuring. Occasional difficulty grasping and holding instruments; occasionally uses topical corticosteroids and hand creams. Asthma improved but persists despite use of non-NRL gloves by all office employees.

Physical Exam: Erythema of fingers and wrists with fine scaling.

Clinical Studies: Patch test: Relevant positive reac-tions to thiuram mix (rubber chemical accelerators, confirmed present in her NRL gloves), glutaraldehyde (active ingredient in cold sterilizing solution used at office), and quaternuim-15 (preservative in hand lotion used by patient). Latex radioallergosorbent test (RAST) (Pharmacia CAP): positive (class 3). Prick test: confirmed allergy to latex, bananas, avocado, house dust mites, and various molds. After patch testing, avoidance of detected allergens (rubber accelerators, glutaraldehyde, quaternium-15) resulted in significant improvement, with continued regular use of moistur-izers and topical steroids. A plateau was reached where symptoms are minimal, and the physical exam reveals only mild erythema and scale between fingers and on dorsal hands.

Diagnosis: Latex allergy and allergic and irritant contact hand eczema.

Impairment Rating: 9% impairment of the whole person. Rating begins in class 1 due to minimal interference with ADLs after allergen identifica-tion and occasional topical medication use. Physical exam findings are in class 2; thus, the rating is raised to 7%. Diagnostic test findings are in class 3 due to multiple relevant positive patch tests and a positive latex prick test. This moves the rating up to the highest category in class 1, 9% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: This case demonstrates the importance of comprehensive patch testing and of not assigning an impairment rating until MMI has been reached. The impairment rating would have been significantly higher if the rating had been determined without first performing patch testing and having the patient avoid the detected allergens. She was also referred to an allergist due to worsening rhinitis, asthma,

and banana allergy. Determine impairment due to rhinitis and asthma separately and combine with skin impairment rating (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix) to determine total impair-ment. All of the patch test reactions are considered as probably relevant, as the exposures were con-firmed and correlated with the site of dermatitis, but no patch testing with the actual substances was carried out to allow assignment of definite relevance. Probably relevant patch test reactions are considered to be RPPTRs, so assigning definite relevance would not affect the rating.

CLASS 2 11% to 27% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 8-9: ATOPIC DERMATITIS

Subject: 44-year-old man.

History: Atopic dermatitis was diagnosed at 2 years of age; asthma developed at age 5, and seasonal rhinitis, at age 11. Treated with topical, inhaled, and nasal steroids throughout childhood, with good dis-ease control. Atopic dermatitis went into remission during adolescence, but symptoms returned in his late 20s with a rash on antecubital fossae, popliteal fossae, and hands. Since then, he has had persistent dermatitis on hands, arms, and legs, with flares lasting 2 to 3 weeks, occurring 1 to 2 times per year, and requiring short courses of systemic steroids. Flares typically occur during allergy season (spring) and involve most of body. Patient requires daily therapy with moisturizers and application of topical steroids approximately 2 weeks per month.

Current Symptoms: Experiences daytime itching that is often worse in evenings and interferes with sleep 3 to 5 times per week. Exercise makes itching and skin symptoms worse, and he is therefore unable to exercise.

Physical Exam: Lichenification of antecubital and popliteal fossae. Redness and scaling of the interdig-ital web spaces and the flexor aspects of the wrists.

Clinical Studies: Elevated IgE level at 0.2 mg/L (246 μg/L); patch tests negative; skin biopsy shows spongiotic dermatitis, consistent with atopic dermatitis.

Diagnosis: Atopic dermatitis.

Impairment Rating: 15% impairment of the whole person. Symptoms are continuously present but are relatively mild and require only intermittent

treatment with prescription topical medications. There is mild interference with several ADLs, including ability to sleep and exercise; therefore, the impairment is initially rated in class 2 at 19%. On exam, less than 10% of the body is involved, hand involvement is minimal, and involvement can usually be concealed, so physical exam is class 1, and the rating changes to 15%. Diagnostic test findings are positive and in the expected range (elevated IgE level and skin biopsy showing spongiotic dermatitis), so diagnostic test findings are class 2 and the impair-ment rating remains at 15%.

Comment: Additional ratings for asthma and sea-sonal rhinitis may be warranted, and if so, would be combined with the skin impairment rating (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix) to deter-mine total impairment.

EXAMPLE 8-10: ATOPIC DERMATITIS

Subject: 25-year-old man.

History: Family history of eczema and hay fever; personal history of infantile eczema with chronic, intermittent, oozing lesions of face, scalp, neck, and upper extremities. Persistent lichenified patches in antecubital, popliteal, and neck areas during remis-sions. Severe exacerbations during high school; fre-quency increased during college.

Current Symptoms: Exacerbations once a month for 7 to 10 days; involves shoulders, arms, hands, legs, and trunk. Eczema during exacerbations limits some ADLs: difficulty sleeping, washing dishes, and con-centrating on complex tasks. Lichenified dermatitis an annoyance but does not significantly limit daily activities. Intermittent application of topical steroid creams during relative remissions. Constant topical steroids, antihistamines, and oatmeal starch baths during flare-ups, which occur monthly. Systemic steroids once a year induce brief remissions.

Physical Exam: Lichenified areas at lateral aspects of neck and arm, leg creases. Erosions, excoriations, erythema, scaling, and crusting of most of the arms and legs also present.

Diagnostic Test Findings: None necessary.

Diagnosis: Atopic dermatitis.

Impairment Rating: 23% impairment of the whole person. Rating begins in class 2 at 19% due to interference with ADLs during flares, which occur approximately 33% of the time. It increases to 23% due to the class 3 physical exam findings of involve-ment of between 20 and 40% of the body. No

diagnostic test findings are necessary, so this does not affect rating, leading to a final rating of 23%.

Comment: Atopic dermatitis exacerbations precipi-tated by variety of agents. Estimated impairment based on essentially constant presence of at least some of signs and symptoms, but only intermittent significant interference with ADLs during flares. Need for and complexity of medical treatment also important. If flared a greater percentage of the time, over 60%, then initial rating would have been in class 3. The IgE level is often checked in patients with atopic dermatitis but is not necessary and is not elevated in all cases, so even if it was checked and was normal, it would not affect the rating.

CLASS 3 30% to 42% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 8-11: ATOPIC DERMATITIS

Subject: 50 year-old woman.

History: Atopic dermatitis beginning in infancy. Required constant therapy with prescription topi-cal agents during childhood and frequent courses of systemic antibiotics and systemic steroids. Disease slowly worsened during adulthood and typically involves most of the body except during aggressive systemic therapy. Current treatment includes pho-totherapy in dermatologist’s office 3 times a week, azathioprine (150 mg/d), nightly soaks in the bath-tub followed by application of heavy emollients or topical steroid ointments, and hydroxyzine (50 mg) before bed. Has improved significantly with this regimen. Treatment regimen and need for controlled environment have resulted in patient being able to work only from home.

Current Symptoms: Continuously itchy and has moderate difficulty sleeping, even while taking hydroxyzine before bed. Skin is continuously scaly and occasionally painful, especially immediately after phototherapy sessions. Sweating makes symp-toms much worse, so she must avoid situations likely to cause sweating. Must also avoid low humidity environments. Unable to shave legs due to dermatitis and worsening of itch. Must wear loose-fitting cotton clothing at all times.

Physical Exam: About one third of the skin of arms and legs is mildly erythematous with moderate scal-ing. There is mild lichenification of the periorbital skin.

Clinical Studies: The IgE level is normal; skin biopsy shows spongiotic dermatitis, consistent with atopic dermatitis.

Impairment Rating: 33% due to atopic dermatitis. Multiple effects on ADLs, including sleep, bathing, clothing selection, environmental restrictions, exer-cise restrictions, employment restrictions, and high BOTC; therefore, initial rating is in class 3 at 36%. Physical exam shows 20% of skin involved, with only mild facial findings, so impairment is rated at class 2 and rating declines to 33%. Although test findings are positive, as expected, with skin biopsy showing spongiotic dermatitis, skin biopsy is not necessary for the diagnosis and is not useful in gaug-ing severity of disease, therefore this does not affect the rating, which remains at 33%.

Comment: In this case, the high BOTC must be considered when determining the initial rating: 3 trips per week to dermatologist’s office for phototherapy, monthly blood tests to monitor for azathioprine toxicity, 30 minutes to an hour spent soaking in bathtub and applying topical medications daily. If more body surface area was involved, could lead to a higher rating.

EXAMPLE 8-12: NAIL DYSTROPHY AND ANONYCHIA

Subject: 40-year-old woman.

History: Swelling, redness of eponychial, paronych-ial areas of all fingers; severe pain, paresthesia after repeated use of sculptured artificial nail kit consist-ing of liquid methylmethacrylate monomer and pow-dered methylmethacrylate polymer. Lost nails on all 10 fingers. Individual observed for several years; no fingernail regrowth.25

Current Symptoms: Persistent paresthesia; diffi-culty grasping small objects such as coins and diffi-culty using many everyday items such as toothbrush, hairbrush, controls on stove, and computer keyboard; cold sensitivity, burning, and tingling. Hand use, in general, aggravates symptoms. Wears adhesive ban-dages over petroleum jelly on nail beds; wears gloves most waking hours. Woman anxious and depressed; requires occasional psychiatric consultation.

Physical Exam: Exposed and keratinized nail beds; paronychial areas swollen and tender.

Clinical Studies: Patch test: Bullous eruption to 2% methylmethacrylate monomer in petrolatum.

Diagnosis: Chemically induced nail dystrophy and anonychia.

Impairment Rating: 30% impairment due to chemi-cally induced nail dystrophy. Significant interference with ADLs is present constantly, leading to initial assignment of class 3 and a rating of 36%. Physical exam findings are in class 2 due to involvement of the hands, and only partial social concealment. Diagnostic test findings are also in class 2 due to presence of RPPTR, so rating changes to 30%.

Comment: Impairment due to neurologic find-ings (paresthesias) could be combined with skin impairment rating (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix) to determine total impairment. Rater should use caution not to double rate the ADL impairment. The AMA Guides Sixth Edition does not recommend additional rating for depression, as the overall effect on ADLs and functioning is reflected in the history.

EXAMPLE 8-13: NEURODERMATITIS AND OCCUPATIONAL CONTACT DERMATITIS

Subject: 45-year-old man.

History: Nurseryman; exposure to many irritant pesticides. Six years’ persistent, pruritic dermatitis involving ankles, forearms, hands, and occasion-ally face and neck. Recurrent pyogenic infection with occasional regional lymph node swelling and tenderness. Dermatitis initially responded to topical therapy and irritant avoidance; condition flared up after re-exposure. Symptoms continued despite job change, avoidance of incriminated agents. No prior dermatologic problems. Symptoms are present every day and require use of topical agents and systemic medication. Noteworthy: 3-year history of headache, memory loss, and anxiety with nausea and vomiting.

Current Symptoms: Neurodermatitis (itch-scratch syndrome). Warm environments, sweating, chemical irritants, and stress provoke severe itching on a daily basis, usually for at least several hours.

Physical Exam: Weeping, excoriated, lichenified plaques and patches of eczema of the face, forearms, and dorsal hands; axillary adenopathy.

Clinical Studies: Patch tests: negative to standard tray and work chemicals. Bacterial culture of skin drainage: Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase positive.

Diagnosis: Persistent neurodermatitis with impetigi-nization secondary to occupational irritant contact dermatitis.

Impairment Rating: 33% impairment due to the skin disorder. The rating begins in class 3 due to the

constant symptoms, need for systemic treatment, and moderate interference with some ADLs and the need to avoid many situations and environments. Dermatitis involves approximately 20% of the body surface, including the face, so physical exam is at class 2 and the impairment rating moves from 36% to 33%. Although there is currently impetiginization, this is a temporary finding and is expected to resolve with appropriate antibiotics, and it therefore does not contribute to the rating. Patch testing is not expected to be positive, as this is a case of irritant dermatitis. Since no diagnostic test findings are expected to be positive, this is not considered in the rating, and the final rating is 33%.

Comment: If a neurologic disorder can be diag-nosed, the attendant impairment should be combined with the skin impairment rating (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix).

EXAMPLE 8-14: THERMAL BURN SCARRING

Subject: 44-year-old man.

History: Burns to palms of both hands during indus-trial accident. Required skin grafts to palms of both hands.

Current Symptoms: Well-healed grafts; residual dryness and cracking, easily injured by minor trauma, noxious chemicals. Bathes, shampoos with gloves on since water and soap irritate hands. Trouble grasping toothbrush, comb, or writing instrument due to cracking, decreased sensation, and skin stiffness. Frequent moisturizer prevents worsen-ing of the symptoms.

Physical Exam: Dry, somewhat atrophic, and stiff grafts on palms of hands.

Clinical Studies: Basic laboratory findings: normal.

Diagnosis: Scarring due to thermal burns.

Impairment Rating: 36% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: There is significant impairment of many ADLs at most times, leading to an initial rating in class 3 at 36%. Physical exam findings involve the entire palms of both hands; thus, the class 3 physical exam finding keeps the rating at 36%. No diagnostic test findings are expected, so this does not affect the rating, leading to a final rating of 36%. Range of motion impairments of the hands can be taken into account if they do not overlap the impairment given for inability to grasp in the skin impairment.

EXAMPLE 8-15: PSORIASIS WITH PUSTULAR FLARES

Subject: 32-year-old man.

History: Initially presented with pretibial erythema-tous, scaly eruption; spread to upper extremities and hand. Pain, swelling, and erythema of knees; sterile urethral discharge. Condition improved only with systemic steroids and cytotoxic agents. Initial pos-sible diagnoses: Reiter’s syndrome, keratoderma blennorrhagica, or pustular psoriasis with psoriatic arthritis. Rehospitalized 3 months later with acute, severely exacerbated skin eruption; severe pain, swell-ing, and deformity of all extremity joints. Over the ensuing year, failed to respond to monotherapy with methotrexate, infliximab, adalimumab, or etanercept. Combination therapy with methotrexate and inflix-imab partially controls disease for the last 2 years.

Current Symptoms: Persistent eruption present on small areas of trunk and extremities. Periodic flare-ups of psoriasis require 5- to 7-day hospitalization 1 to 2 times per year, and it takes up to 1 month to return to baseline disease. Exacerbations with generalized pustulation involve 100% of BSA and are associated with fevers, chills, and generalized malaise. During acute phase of flare-ups it is dif-ficult to care for himself, stand, sit, walk, or drive, leading to brief hospitalization. At baseline, involved skin is itchy and painful, and it is difficult to sit or drive for long periods. Skin regularly bleeds, cracks, and flakes, which limits ability to perform activi-ties such as doing laundry and outdoor maintenance of home.

Physical Exam: Red, scaly plaques with adherent silvery scale present over 60% of the body. Pitting of the nails is noted.

Clinical Studies: Biopsy: Extreme thickening of the stratum corneum and many neutrophils in the stra-tum corneum.

Diagnosis: Psoriasis with pustular flares.

Impairment Rating: 39% impairment due to psoria-sis. Disease is present 100% of the time, but severe flares of skin disease are present 1 to 2 months per year. If there were no severe flares, one could consider class 2, whereas if the disease flared all the time, class 4 would be appropriate, Therefore, assigned class 3, 36%, initially based on presence of regular severe flares and continued presence of moderate disease between flares. Necessity for continuous therapy with multiple systemic agents also contributes to rating in class 3 rather than class 2. Physical exam findings show involvement of 60% of BSA, which supports a rating in class 4, which increases rating to 39%.

Biopsy, although consistent with psoriasis, is not nec-essary for the diagnosis and is not a useful indicator of disease severity, so diagnostic test findings do not contribute to the rating, which remains at 39%.

Comment: Radiologic findings and joint symptoms and signs should be considered and rated separately from skin disease and combined with skin rating (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix) to determine whole person impairment.

EXAMPLE 8-16: SKIN CANCER

Subject: 40-year-old man.

History: Laborer; noted to have multiple basal cell carcinomas since age 15 years involving both exposed and covered body areas. History of cardiac fibromas.

Current Symptoms: Multiple weeping, oozing, ulcerated lesions on trunk present at all times; reclu-sive behavior because of inability to go into the sun. Need for continuous surgical removal of skin tumors, continuous application of antibiotic ointments, and application of dressings to ulcerated skin cancers.

Physical Exam: More than 50 nodular and ulcerated dome-shaped tumors of face and trunk with serosan-guineous foul-smelling drainage; some tumors larger than 5 cm in diameter. Palmar and plantar pits and facial milia.

Clinical Studies: Skin biopsies: basal cell carci-noma. Radiographs: macrocephaly, hypertelorism, frontal bossing, odontogenic keratocysts of the jaws, calcification of the falx cerebri, and bifid ribs.

Diagnosis: Basal cell nevus syndrome with multiple basal cell carcinomas.

Impairment Rating: 42% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: Although there is a lack of pain and only a moderate level of interference with physical abil-ity ADLs, the BOTC, due to dressings and frequent surgeries, is extremely high and affects ability to perform ADLs, as does need to avoid sun. Initial rating, therefore, is in class 3. Thus, the rating begins at 36%. Physical exam findings are in class 4, as over 40% of the body has at least minimal involve-ment or residual scarring and the findings cannot be concealed; the rating therefore increases to 39%. Multiple diagnostic test findings are positive (many skin biopsies, radiographs), and diagnostic test find-ings are therefore rated class 4, and the final rating is 42%. If metastatic disease develops, rating would automatically increase to 58%.

CLASS 4 45% to 58% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 8-17: FOLLICULAR OCCLUSIVE TRIAD

Subject: 28-year-old man.

History: A 12-year history of acne vulgaris, hidradenitis suppurativa, and dissecting cellulitis of the scalp (follicular occlusive triad). Temporary improvement with topical and systemic antibiotics, intralesional corticosteroids, aspiration, marsupial-ization, zinc sulfate, and 2 courses of isotretinoin. Over last 5 years, large cystic lesions developed, mainly involving posterior scalp, face, neck, upper part of the trunk, axilla, and inguinal area.

Current Symptoms: Lesions accompanied by fever and aching joints. Large lesions on back, chest, and scalp and in the inguinal area make resting difficult in warm weather. Clothing and sweating aggravate disorder. Due to severe axillary and groin pain when moving arms and legs, he has severe difficulty with many household and personal care activities. Due to pain and exudate from abscesses, he is unable to participate in some social and recreational activities.

Physical Exam: Inflamed cystic lesions located on posterior scalp, face, neck, upper trunk, axilla, and inguinal area. Skin severely scarred.

Clinical Studies: White blood cell (WBC) count is between 18 and 22.0 × 109 L (18 to 22.0 × 103/μL) on multiple lab tests.

Diagnosis: Acne conglobata; hidradenitis suppu-rativa; dissecting cellulitis of the scalp; severe scar formation.

Impairment Rating: 48% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: Many ADLs affected constantly. Requires frequent systemic medications. These fac-tors lead to initial rating in class 4 at 51%. Physical exam findings involve 20% to 40% of the body, and the odor and exudate are sometimes difficult to con-ceal, leading to a rating in class 3, which changes the impairment rating to 48%. Repeated elevated WBC count is an unexpected finding and indicates severe disease, so diagnostic test findings are in class 4, leading to a final rating of 48%. Radical excision of affected areas might lead to improve-ment. If this happened, would be appropriate to reconsider rating.

EXAMPLE 8-18: PEMPHIGUS VULGARIS

Subject: 35-year-old man.

History: Persistently sore mouth for 22 months. Vesicles and bullae over face, trunk, and extremities. High doses of oral corticosteroids administered to control disease.

Current Symptoms: Persistent blisters and erosions result in chronic, unremitting pain on swallowing or speaking. Erosions and skin fragility involving mouth, trunk, and genital area; unable to have sexual intercourse, eat solid foods, brush teeth, speak above a whisper, or sleep well. Azathioprine therapy added to high-dose corticosteroids; limited disease control. Complex therapy requires frequent physician visits for checkups and laboratory monitoring.

Physical Exam: Many eroded lesions of tongue and oral mucous membranes; lesions over trunk and extremities. Infected bullae of mouth and trunk.

Clinical Studies: White blood cell count: leuko-penia (secondary to therapy). Biopsy: pemphigus vulgaris with positive immunofluorescence and high titers of desmoglein antibodies.

Diagnosis: Pemphigus vulgaris.

Impairment Rating: 51% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: Severe interference with most ADLs due to lesions and pemphigus pain, despite continuous systemic therapy. These factors lead to initial assign-ment of class 4 and a rating of 51%. More than 40% of the BSA is involved, so physical exam is also in class 4, but severity of oral involvement argues for increase to 54%. Positive skin biopsy and immunofluorescence are expected. High titer of desmoglein antibodies despite therapy is unexpected and indicates severe dis-ease, so diagnostic test findings are class 3 and final rating is 51%. Laboratory findings of leukopenia are rated separately in the hematology chapter (Chapter 9) and combined using the Combined Values Chart (see Appendix). Experimental new therapeutic modalities, such as rituximab or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), could lead to improvement in condition. If this occurred, reassessment of impairment would be appropriate.

EXAMPLE 8-19: THERMAL BURN SCARRING AND DYSPNEA

Subject: 25-year-old man.

History: Three years ago suffered severe burns over 85% of total BSA and smoke inhalation; some skin grafts.

Current Symptoms: Unable to work with heavy equipment. Skin fragile, dried, and cracked. Hot, dizzy, and unable to perspire in warm environ-ments. Marked difficulty with writing, walking, and nonspecific hand activities due to stiff, shiny skin. Scar formation causes pain and decreased range of motion. Feels disfigured. Greatly limited ability to participate in group activities. No sexual relations after injury; short of breath with physical activity.

Physical Exam: Healed atrophic scars over 85% of body; minimally atrophic skin grafts and donor sites. Several depigmented areas, including some on cheeks and backs of hands. Partial destruction of left ear; distorted fingernails. Diminished range of motion of both hands.

Clinical Studies: Basic laboratory findings: normal.

Diagnosis: Extensive scarring due to thermal burns and dyspnea.

Impairment Rating: 58% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: Continuous, severe interference with ADLs is present, leading to initial rating in class 4 at 51%. Also, 85% BSA involved, including several facial and hand areas. Physical exam rating is in class 4, but severity of involvement leads to increase of rating to highest level, 58%. Diagnostic test find-ings are not expected or necessary, so no effect on rating from diagnostic test findings, leading to final rating of 58%. Combine the skin (burn) impair-ment with impairments due to musculoskeletal and pulmonary dysfunction (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix) to determine whole person impairment.

EXAMPLE 8-20: MYCOSIS FUNGOIDES

Subject: 56-year-old man.

History: Over 20 years, progressive pruritic rash; pruritic patches on back and extremities. Topical therapy; eruption gradually generalized. Treated with topical nitrogen mustard, PUVA, photophoresis, and electron beam therapy. Eruption uncontrolled with cytotoxic agent or radiation therapy.

Current Symptoms: Confined to home; unable to care for himself, walk, travel, grasp, or participate in sexual activity.

Physical Exam: Diffuse, erythematous, scaly plaques; some quite firm. Many trunk and extrem-ity excoriations; foul-smelling and draining nodular tumors on face, palms, and soles. Palpable axillary and inguinal lymph nodes.

Clinical Studies: Biopsy: skin, lymph node positive for mycosis fungoides. Other lab findings: normal.

Diagnosis: Mycosis fungoides.

Impairment Rating: 100% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: Mycosis fungoides is a form of lym-phoma, and as per the rating table, any malignancy (other than basal cell carcinoma) that is not in remis-sion automatically qualifies for 58% impairment. The 58% skin impairment would be combined with other system impairments. However, this patient has termi-nal disease at this point and is undergoing palliative therapy only, therefore, the rating goes to 100%.

EXAMPLE 8-21: XERODERMA PIGMENTOSUM

Subject: 18-year-old woman.

History: Photophobia for 13 years. At 5 years of age, marked pigmentation of sun-exposed areas of face, chest, arms, and legs. Since then, generalized freckling of skin, several areas of telangiectasia, and multiple basal cell carcinomas and multiple SCCs (squamous cell carcinomas) that are appearing and growing too rapidly to allow curative therapy.

Current Symptoms: Condition progressing in severity; continuous observation and treatment. Confined to home for past year.

Physical Exam: Multiple large, nodular, ulcerated tumors in all sun exposed areas. Some keratinized, some black. Extreme freckling, scaling, and skin fragility in all sun exposed skin that is not involved with tumor. Face is the worst area, exposed arms also involved.

Clinical Studies: Basic lab findings: normal. Fecal, urinary porphyrin studies: negative. Multiple biopsies and excisions showing basal cell carcinoma, SCC, and melanoma.

Diagnosis: Xeroderma pigmentosum.

Impairment Rating: 100% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: Has active SCC that is not curable, and as per the rating table, any malignancy (other than basal cell carcinoma) that is not in remission would automatically qualify for a rating of 58%. However, this patient has terminal disease and would therefore be rated at 100%.

EXAMPLE 8-22: EPIDERMOLYSIS BULLOSA DYSTROPHICA

Subject: 19-year-old man.

History: Bullous lesions and open wounds devel-oped shortly after birth and have been continuously present since then, despite extreme lifestyle altera-tions designed to minimize cutaneous trauma. Bullae appeared after slightest trauma; healed with severe scarring and milia. Fingers and toes have fused into mitten and sock deformities. Several operations to release fingers have been of only temporary benefit, and patient currently has no use of hands.

Current Symptoms: Requires continuous assis-tance, as he is unable to perform any ADLs.

Physical Exam: Fingers are fused, tapered stumps (mitten deformities for hands). Constant bullae in mouth and pharynx; probably extended to epiglottis. Over half of body involved with erosions and scarring, requiring extensive bandaging 100% of the time. Weight 40% below desirable for height.

Clinical Studies: Roentgenography: esophageal stricture. Complete blood cell count: Iron deficiency anemia and anemia of chronic disease. Albumin level: 26 g/L (2.6 g/dL). Wound cultures yielded methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) that is sensitive to clindamycin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Prior skin biopsy showed subepidermal split.

Diagnosis: Epidermolysis bullosa dystrophica.

Impairment Rating: 58% impairment due to epidermolysis bullosa dystrophica.

Comment: This autosomal recessive disorder is one of the most impairing of all hereditary diseases; impairment approaches 100% and death. In this case, due to extreme interference with ADLs, initial rating is class 4 at 51%. Extreme nature of physical findings leads to increase of rating to 54%. Multiple diagnostic test findings, including skin biopsy, iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, low albumin level, and positive wound cultures lead to class 4 rating and a final rating of 58% for this skin disease. Combine with impairment estimates for esophageal stricture, anemia, and any other related musculoskeletal and internal medicine impairments (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix) to determine whole person impairment.
